For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment. Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me. Behold, you delight in truth in the inward being, and you teach me wisdom in the secret heart. Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones that you have broken rejoice. Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit. Then I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners will return to you. Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, O God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness. O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise. For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise. $AVGO earnings call highlights !

$AVGO CEO: On adding up his own two-year AI shipment guide
"It will be 30 GW between the customers we have, the six customers we have. Question is, will all 30 come into production within these two fiscal years? We are giving you a judged number of $115 billion of chips to these guys in fiscal 2027, another $230 billion in 2028, which would add up, I know, to about $350 billion. Another way of saying is, we believe with a pretty high degree of confidence, we will ship $350 billion of AI semiconductors to these customers in the next two years. That's the best way to look at it. It doesn't necessarily mean all 30 GW need to have been deployed within that period.… As I said, when you do an XPU, it not only performs as well, if not better, for your particular LLM workloads for each of our customers, it's also half the cost. In fact, less than half the cost. You made my point exactly." — Hock Tan, President and CEO

$AVGO CEO: On why demand isn't the constraint — capacity is
"Whatever I tell you guys go out and print a bigger number. I think that's funny. We are very careful, and to be honest, we try to be conservative. So we are giving you an outlook. Yeah, demand, we can ship significantly more. Question in our mind sometimes is, even as we ship the chips, are they going to be deployed on a timely basis? That's always very much in our mind when we give you that outlook. But certainly our customers want us to ship more. But we have secured supply, and we think it's the right number to put it to 115. If times, if circumstances change and our ability to scale more supply change, of course we will uplift. But at this point, that's our best outlook. And by the way, the same thinking applies to 2028 when we give you that outlook of $230 billion. This is real demand, we believe, based on what's available, what data center sites, locations are ready 2028 with respect to our customers, the size of what we have, and against the supply chain we have in leading edge wafers, substrates, and HBM memory. This is again, a carefully structured outlook that we believe we can achieve." — Hock Tan, President and CEO

$AVGO CEO: On the actual bottleneck — land, power, shell, and everything else
"That's a hell of a question, and you're right in all counts. It's a multidimensional issue to get an AI data center deployed. We now are all more sensitive about, especially at scale, and we are now delivering at scale to our customers XPU AI data center built upon XPU computing accelerators. Land, power, and shell, as I indicated to a question with Will, is a big concern. More than a big concern, it dictates specific timing of when this capacity gets deployed and be available. But very much in the mix that we have to think about with our customers, and it's a joint collaborative effort, not just one direction, is, you said it correctly, leading-edge silicon. Because for one, to get the chip produced and availability of those chips and the time it comes in. Then even deeper than that, we talk about substrates, which is a specific issue, which is leading us to build our own substrate capacity at scale in our factory in Singapore, jointly with one of our partners. Of course, we all know about memory, HBM memory. Beyond HBM memory, the system memory that goes into AI servers, which we don't supply necessarily, but our customers have to secure too. All these are multidimensional problem coming from various sources, depending on different times, each might become a bottleneck. It's a constant interesting challenge as we work this through, which is why, in some ways, I'm so glad we have only six customers to deal with." — Hock Tan, President and CEO

$AVGO CEO: On why he's confident Anthropic and OpenAI will keep buying
"Don't forget, with the rate of growth, these startups, and we are talking about we have six customers, and we are creating these financial vehicles, as Amie described them, for just two of them, not all. The other four customers of ours are financially secure, stable enough to be able to fund it themselves, and we are happy for them to do that and get them up to where they need to with sheer technology, which we have in plentiful supply. With these two guys, Anthropic and OpenAI, it is like thinking of you have two geniuses in the middle of, what? Outer Mongolia, say, and they need to go to college to fulfill where they want to. We do what we can to help them, and part of it is creating sources of financing to help these companies with the leading-edge frontier models in the world be able to play in the same playing field and be able to offer these great technology products to the world. That is simply what we are doing. It is a great investment for us when you think about it, that every gigawatt of compute they deploy, they could achieve $30 billion of ARR, annual revenue per gigawatt. That is a hell of a business model. For us, that is a great investment to focus on doing. To put that simply, that is how we look at this simple thing. It makes economic sense for Broadcom to invest and enable these guys. These guys are going to be hyperscalers in their own right. What they do is they want first-party compute capacity. Just as they want to create silicon that is very cost performance optimized, and they want to run their own data centers eventually first hand. Not even eventually. They want to run it as fast as they can. Short term, you are right. They are using cloud services, third-party services to deploy their models. Long term, we see these guys to be no different from a hyperscaler and will run their own data centers and be first party to offer AI, generative AI, APIs, as SaaS models to the world. We see that happening. It is not speculation, it is actually happening, and we are in the midst of enabling that." — Hock Tan, President and CEO

$AVGO CFO: On the correction to her own gross margin number

"First, I want to just make sure I correct what I said before, just to be super crisp. Gross margin for our Semiconductor Solutions segment was approximately 67% in Q3. To your question, gross margin really reflects revenue mix between both semiconductors and infrastructure software. Then within semiconductors, the product mix is reflected, as well as increasing memory content. As you can see, as XPUs become a larger proportion of our total revenue mix, it impacts our margin. We guide one quarter at a time, so we will tell you each quarter what our margin is going to look like." — Amie Thuener, CFO

$AVGO CEO: On why gross margin is the wrong number to watch
"It is not the first time we have told you guys that, because stop focusing on gross margin is what we are saying. Look at where it matters, operating margin at the end of the day, because the growth in revenue far surpasses their growth in OpEx, operating spending, to support their growth in revenue. We have a lot of accretion, operating leverage, we call it, on operating margin. We expect to be able to sustain operating margin even as mix of products dilutes the gross margin." — Hock Tan, President and CEO

$AVGO CFO: On what the backstop financing actually is — and isn't
"We don't have anything to announce today on residual value guarantees or backstop. There's nothing new to add. The numbers that you outlined around what we've already done remain true. As I mentioned in my prepared remarks, we're going to evaluate any strategic financing really on a deal-by-deal basis. We expect that any that we do in the future, they're going to have unique features, and they're going to be tailored specifically to the lab and to the investor needs. I can't give you an overarching look at what's the max and what each one's going to look like. But we will tell you at the right time. We have nothing to announce today." — Amie Thuener, CFO

$AVGO CEO: On why dollars per gigawatt should hold steady
"Which means there are less of it of a more advanced XPU in 1 GW. So what we are seeing per gigawatt is in the range of less than $30 billion, $20 billion-$30 billion per gigawatt. And we expect that to be very sustaining in that level because the power of each chip goes up. So even as you increase the price of the chip, the content in dollars is relatively stable. Just accept the fact that there's going to be a lot more gigawatts out there. But the dollars per gigawatt will remain in the $20 billion-$30 billion level of our content. But we have seen and we expect to see an acceleration in the number of gigawatts just to address the exponential compute demand required by our customers." — Hock Tan, President and CEO

$AVGO President, Semiconductor Solutions: On Tomahawk 6 and Tomahawk Ultra adoption
"You are right. Our Tomahawk 6 has been a phenomenal success. It started really first in scale-out, as you mentioned. It is available both in 100 Gb and 200 Gb SerDes. We actually have two versions of Tomahawk 6. Both are very successful and both are deployed in pretty much all of the AI hyperscalers that are building XPUs with us, and even those that are not using our XPUs are using the Tomahawk 6, both 100 Gb and 200 Gb. With respect to Tomahawk Ultra, we have quite innovated ahead of the market here by enabling scale-up using low latency Ethernet. The adoption also on this device has surprised us, and we are starting to see it deployed, starting actually this quarter and in FY 2027 coming up in scale-up applications." — Charlie Kawwas, President, Semiconductor Solutions Group

$AVGO President, Semiconductor Solutions: On why customers standardize on Broadcom networking once they pick an XPU
"On the attach rate for scale up, today we're actually seeing customers who build XPUs with us deploy either Tomahawk 6, they used to deploy Tomahawk 5, now they're going to Tomahawk 6, and some of them are going to Tomahawk Ultra. If you look at where we're seeing XPUs and even GPUs, we're seeing scale-up solutions adopt both Tomahawk 6 and Tomahawk Ultra. The beauty and the reason why they're doing this, as Hock articulated earlier on, it's Ethernet based, which means it's open. Anybody can connect to it, especially with the standards that we have collaborated with the entire industry on. At this point in time, we're seeing it pretty much deployed in both XPU clusters and in some GPU clusters." — Charlie Kawwas, President, Semiconductor Solutions Group

$AVGO CEO: On Google, Anthropic and OpenAI's separate multi-year gigawatt paths
"We believe the vast majority of compute demand for AI workloads today originates from this concentrated group who develops state-of-the-art frontier models. We expect their need for compute infrastructure to inflate even more in 2027 and 2028. They are all growing with XPUs to achieve superior performance, cost, and power. Let me now walk you through each of our customer's journey towards using XPUs at scale to run their frontier models worldwide. Our workloads, sorry. Our engagement with Google has never been stronger. This has been recently strengthened by a long-term agreement to develop and supply future generations of TPUs and AI networking. Under this agreement, we're planning to deliver multi-tens of billions of dollars of TPUs annually over the next several years. We expect this growing demand in 2028 and 2029 to be fulfilled through successive generations of the increasingly complex TPUs we are developing today with Google. Our partnership with Google will continue to sustain because we have the strongest IP portfolio in semiconductor design, including industry-leading SerDes, chip-to-chip interconnect, leading-edge HBM and SRAM integration, and simply differentiated advanced packaging. Most of all, we have consistently, I should say, delivered the fastest time to market for TPUs from product definition to production without the need for respins. We believe these are very deep moats for any competitor to cross. Moving on to Anthropic. Starting with the 1 GW of Ironwood we are deploying in 2026, we expect Anthropic to deploy another 5 GW of TPU v8i in 2027. In 2028, we have clear line of sight to deliver an incremental 10 GW, even as we expect Google to grow for us. Anthropic is on track to become our largest XPU customer in 2027 and sustain that in 2028. For OpenAI, Jalapeño is on track for the planned deployment of 1.3 GW in 2027. Together with OpenAI, we are deep in development of the next generation XPU beyond Jalapeño, which is approaching tape-out. In 2028, we have line of sight for OpenAI to deploy over 5 GW of Jalapeño and its successor generation of XPU, which would make OpenAI our second-largest XPU customer." — Hock Tan, President and CEO

$AVGO CFO: On what the XPV financing platform actually does
"In June, we established the AI XPV Platform in partnership with Apollo and Blackstone to enable more than 20 GW of compute infrastructure for OpenAI and Anthropic by the end of 2028. We closed the first $35 billion tranche in June for Anthropic's 1 GW deployment, which is already underway. While future tranches will include unique features tailored to specific lab and investor needs, our core strategy remains consistent. First, we are empowering two of our most strategic customers, the leading AI labs, to bridge the gap between their current cash flow and the significant upfront investments required for their businesses. Our XPUs enable cost-effective, sustainable growth at multiples of their infrastructure costs. Second, this XPV Platform enables highly investable customers and facilitates execution where demand is already locked in. Third, we review any strategic financings through a commercial as well as balance sheet lens, consistent with our existing capital allocation framework. Through the XPV Platform, we partner with sophisticated third-party financial partners to independently underwrite and capitalize the assets, rather than providing the direct financing ourselves. Where necessary, we may provide modest residual value guarantees, which are contingent liabilities we view as low risk, supported by the strong profitability trajectory of these labs and the sustaining value of the underlying assets." — Amie Thuener, CFO

$AVGO CEO: On what's actually being built ahead of schedule
"At the same time, we began production shipments of the next generation TPU v8i for Google. This new TPU generation has been designed with more memory and bandwidth compared to Ironwood and just like Ironwood, is optimized for inference workloads. In performance it is comparable, if not surpasses the Vera Rubin GPU. Just to reiterate the major technology challenges of developing these complex accelerators, Broadcom is now shipping the TPU v8i ahead of the MediaTek version v8t, which in fact was initiated earlier. In Q3, we also ship Jalapeño, OpenAI's first generation custom accelerator, which outperforms Grace Blackwell GPU for inference workloads. Overall, our XPU shipments for the third quarter were up over 3.5 x year-on-year and represented 73% of AI revenue during the quarter. Our AI networking revenue was up over 2.5 x year-on-year." — Hock Tan, President and CEO

text:
Ben’s desk, Saturday 5 Sep. Catch the audience up without picking a choir.
The post: Climate Change Authority call is “a joke.” They treat worry about the power bill as climate misinformation. Listen here. That is the fight as 2GB frames it. The map underneath is older than the segment.

What actually printed
August 2026, Climate Change Authority insights paper: Misinformation: A climate policy risk.
It does not say, in one sentence, “your Origin bill is a lie.” It does something more useful to an office. It lists the new shape of “misinformation” after denial got tired:

cost of living
energy prices and reliability
jobs
regional impacts
biodiversity
whether Australia’s action even matters

Those are the things a household actually meets. The paper then says those narratives delay projects, raise costs, and divide communities — so a cross-agency working group will “address” them. DCCEEW already stood one up. Annual Progress Advice will flag the risk. That is a thicker certificate.
Plain English: if the meter is the argument, the meter can be classed as a narrative. That is the joke Ben heard. It is also the loop.

Lack of choice in your choice
You are offered two names.
Climate gain. Sing the hymn. Renewables are cheapest. 1.5 was the fight for humanity. Overshoot-and-removal is the new fight. The bill will come down later (Reputex once said $275 a year cheaper by 2025; AEMC later said unit cost could be about 13 percent lower in ten years if the rollout lands). Your job is to wait, comply, and treat the neighbour who points at the invoice as the delay.
Climate loss. Call the hymn a lie. Florida-underwater-in-2000. Grain of salt. The working group is a ministry of truth. Your job is to pick the other banner.
Governance gain is both.

Gain-side: targets, working group, social-licence paper, removal market, data-centre 100 percent renewable rule unless a utility proves fossil is cheaper. Office keeps G.
Loss-side: “misinformation” as the parent of the bill. Same office keeps G. The choir still pays E and D_seq — the leftover on the meter, the regional fight, the next seal.

There is no third checkout. Refusal is still a post on the same tape. That is what “no outside family by refusing the hymn” means in talkback: you can bag Bowen on air and still be priced as refusal. You can bag Fordham on air and still be priced as compliance. The book clears either way.
dR/dt = G(R) − E(t) − D_seq(t)
G is the going concern: CCA advice, minister, retailer, certificate.
E is exported onto the household that did not write the paper.
D_seq is this week’s extra seal: the bill itself rebadged as a narrative risk.

eta greater than 1: the loop is on. Shortfall invoiced to the choir. Not cheaper electrons as delivery. The invoice as heartbeat.

Two offices, one meter
Climate Change Authority / DCCEEW / minister — own the target and the misinfo paper.

AEMO / AEMC / retailers / poles and wires — own the price that lands. ACCC has already said millions of households pay a “loyalty tax” for not switching. That is a different leftover. Do not glue it to “renewables” or to “denial” as a single parent. Stack it.

The electron does not honour the split. Neither does the quarterly.
Wrong wave: “cheapest form of energy” as a slogan versus the hour the network, firming, transmission blowouts, and retail margins actually print. Same class of sentence as Keelung’s 70 mm hour versus a 76 mm/h pipe — a spec that did not swallow the event.

Thread dynamics (do not become the replies)
Ben: joke, listen to the show. Certificate of outrage. Useful as a pointer at the paper. Not a completed physics.

Reply A: globalists, foreign powers, satanic add-on. That is a detonator plaque. It deletes the meter. Do not mint it.
Reply B: screenshots, no sentence. Choir with pictures.
UNEP two days earlier (the “humanity speeding past the limit” post): 1.5 is retired; overshoot-and-return is the new title; carbon removal is the new product. Australia’s working group is the local spelling of that replacement seal. Climate-gain and climate-loss both sell the next seal. That is governance gain.
Catch-up for anyone who only heard the grab
Bills are a number on a page. Calling the worry “misinformation” does not change the number.

Promised $275 off by 2025 was a model, not a refund.

Some retail extra is just old-plan inertia. That is not a climate particle and not a denial particle.
Some system cost is poles, firming, delays, and targets. That is also not a slogan.
The office wins if you only pick a side. Gain-policy and loss-policy are two prices for keeping the radius.
Ice in Nepal, a dike in Putian, a viaduct in Buffalo, a drain in Keelung — those are cascades. This paper is a certificate. Stack them. Do not let Canberra author Lhende. Do not let Lhende author your bill.
Sockets that do not reset when the talkback reset
Leftover after the license is debt.

Dual quote: bid / offer, for / against, on one tape.

Names reset (1.5, cheapest, misinfo, $275). The meter and the unused warning do not have to.
Closing a false fold does not delete c.
Look at the feet. The feet are a cut. The bill is a cut. The working group is a plaque on top of the cut.
the form was never divided

The Right’s Top 10 | Friday, September 4, 2026, 08:43 PM  🦅

Leading Issues for Americans in Early September 2026: A Synthesis of Polling from Gallup, Pew, AP-NORC, and Others.  

Execute an unyielding, comprehensive summary of the top national headlines for September 4, 2026, anchored strictly in reporting from leading conservative and center-right outlets.

Prominent headlines from September 4, 2026, drawn from Fox News, The Wall Street Journal, New York Post, Newsmax, Epoch Times, Washington Examiner, Daily Caller, Breitbart, and similar outlets. Stories reflect widely reported factual developments that day.

Foreign Policy/Conflicts (dominant story)

The U.S.-Iran military campaign, now in its seventh month after beginning in late February, remained the top story. Vice President JD Vance, in the first White House press briefing in weeks, declined to call the fighting a “war,” saying major combat operations lasted about six weeks and that there is currently “no active shooting,” even as exchanges continued around the Strait of Hormuz and Iran targeted commercial shipping. He refused to set a timeline for an end, saying it depends on Iran stopping attacks on ships, and expressed skepticism about Iranian reports that a U.S. strike hit a wedding, killing five including a child. President Trump later described the conflict as “small potatoes.”  ⁠Fox News

U.S. diesel prices hit a record $5.85 per gallon amid energy-market disruptions from the fighting. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced additional sanctions targeting Iran’s shadow oil fleet and officials. Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were slated to travel for Ukraine-related talks with Russia. The U.S. military reported downing about 100 suspected cartel drones at the southern border in August. The Coast Guard intercepted a vessel and recovered 47 bales of suspected marijuana valued at $2.4 million.  ⁠Newsmax

Government Dysfunction/Poor Leadership/Political Division/Corruption

The Missouri Supreme Court blocked GOP-backed congressional maps ahead of the midterms; Trump called the ruling “ridiculous.” The Trump administration proposed stripping tax-exempt status from schools using race-based programs. A federal judge extended a block on U.S. Postal Service mail-in ballot restrictions (envelope standards, barcodes, data uploads) as the White House sought Supreme Court intervention before ballots go out. The House had canceled its last two weeks of September session. Fox News parted ways with longtime anchor Maria Bartiromo; Trump praised her as a “true warrior.” The Lindsay Clancy murder trial in Massachusetts ended in a mistrial after a deadlock and a defense request to remove a holdout juror. Reports highlighted Medicare and Medicaid fraud estimated at $1 million per minute.  ⁠Fox News

Immigration

Coverage emphasized southern-border drone intercepts by the U.S. military and ICE-related cases, including an officer released on bond in a Minneapolis shooting matter and a guilty plea in a cartel border-tunnel case. A father whose daughter was murdered criticized Chicago sanctuary policies. DHS sought faster dismissal of certain asylum claims.  Fox News

Crime/Violence/Gun Violence/Drug Addiction

Officials identified victims in a Minneapolis apartment shooting that also injured officers. A 70-year-old Florida woman opened fire inside a police department lobby. NYPD fatally shot a knife-wielding man on the Brooklyn Bridge. Andrew Tate was indicted in Romania on trafficking and related charges. Drug interdiction appeared in the Coast Guard marijuana seizure.  NY Post

National Unity/Polarization/State of Democracy

Redistricting fights (Missouri map blocked; Maryland ballot measure allowed) and mail-in voting litigation dominated pre-midterm coverage. The House passed a bill targeting federal funding for colleges that boycott Israel, with some Democratic support. A Chicago socialism conference featuring masks and speakers such as Hasan Piker drew criticism as evidence of left-wing radicalism. Midterm campaigning and polarization over the Iran conflict and voting rules were recurring themes.  Breitbart

Health Care Costs/Affordability/Cost of Living

Record diesel prices ($5.85/gallon) and elevated energy costs from the Iran conflict were cited as driving transportation and inflation pressures. Trump signed orders aimed at easing beef prices through processing changes and country-of-origin labeling. Wage growth (about 3.1% year-over-year) lagged inflation in some reports. House Democrats discussed healthcare expansion.  ⁠Theepochtimes

Economy/Federal Budget Deficit/National Debt

The August jobs report showed +162,000 nonfarm payrolls (well above forecasts of ~53,000–65,000), unemployment unchanged at 4.1%, and upward revisions to prior months. Gains were concentrated in food service and local-government education. Markets fell as the strong data raised odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike; Trump called for the Fed to cut rates instead. Mortgage rates had recently hit a one-year high amid bond-market pressure tied to deficits and energy prices. National debt concerns and canceled House work on related issues were noted. Dell stock surged on AI demand.  ⁠Forbes

Poverty/Homelessness/Related Social Issues

Limited dedicated coverage on September 4 from these outlets; stories more often tied social issues to sanctuary-city crime, rural hospital access, or broader cost-of-living pressures from energy prices rather than standalone homelessness reporting.  

Overall Daily Summary

Anna Paulina Luna (née Mayerhofer; born May 6, 1989) is an American politician and Air Force veteran serving as the U.S. representative for Florida's 13th congressional district since 2023. A member of the Republican Party, she is the first Mexican-American woman elected to Congress from Florida.

Luna served as airfield management specialist in the Air National Guard from age 19, serving from 2009 to 2014. For her service, she was awarded the Air Force Achievement Medal.[1] Luna graduated from the University of West Florida in 2017. In her first campaign, Luna challenged, and lost to, incumbent Democratic congressman Charlie Crist in 2020. Luna was subsequently elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 2022, with the endorsement of then-former president Donald Trump in the Republican primary. Luna was re-elected in 2024.

Luna serves on the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. During her congressional tenure, Luna has maintained a conservative voting record of 98%, according to Heritage Action.[2]

Early life and family
Anna Paulina Mayerhofer was born on May 6, 1989, to George Mayerhofer and Monica Todd, an elementary school teacher and stay-at-home mother, in Santa Ana, California.[3][4][5][6] Luna has said that her father raised her to follow Messianic Judaism, an evangelical movement that incorporates Jewish traditions into Protestant Christianity, and that she is "a small fraction Ashkenazi".[5][7][8][9] Members of her extended family have denied this claim, saying her father was Catholic, and that "they were not aware of him practicing any form of Judaism while Luna was growing up".[5] Her mother has said that Luna's father was a Christian who "embraced the Messianic faith" after getting clean from drug addiction. Her grandfather, Heinrich Mayerhofer, identified as Catholic when he immigrated to Canada from Germany in 1954.[5][10]

Her father had Mexican and German ancestry. Her paternal grandmother was born in Hidalgo, Mexico. Her paternal grandfather was born in Germany and was in the Wehrmacht during World War II.[5] Her mother has Mexican-American ancestry,[5] although a maternal great-grandfather was the son of an American immigrant to Mexico and a native of Colima, Mexico.[11] Her two maternal great-grandfathers served in the United States Armed Forces during World War II.[5]

Luna's parents never married or lived together;[6] her father had a drug addiction problem,[5] her mother married another man when Luna was nine years old but divorced four years later.[6] Luna was raised in the Orange County cities of Santa Ana, Irvine, and Aliso Viejo, as well as Los Angeles, and has called Santa Monica her hometown.[12] She attended high school in Los Angeles.[3][5]

Luna said that at the age of 10, she found her father's bag of meth.[3] Her maternal grandmother was a long-time heroin user and was HIV positive.[5][13] By 2020, she (Anna) and her mother (Monica) had chosen the Luna surname as "an homage" to that woman's maiden name.[5][13]

Luna has said that she "grew up in the welfare system",[14] raised by her mother on government assistance with "no family to rely on", and was raised in a "broken home mentality".[5] Luna has said that both she and her mother lacked "a strong extended network of people" who could help care for them,[5] and that she had attended "over six high schools" before graduating.[3] Luna's cousin has said, "The whole family kind of raised her—my dad was a part of her life when she was younger and we all kind of coddled her ... She was always a part of everything, all these family gatherings and activities". Luna's aunt said, "She had everything. What she needed and more ... And not only did [Luna's mother] provide for her, but [Luna's grandfather] did, too."[5] Luna has disputed these accounts, saying that she "barely spent any time with them in her entire life". Luna's mother said that she (Monica) had to rely on welfare for periods of time, especially while she was putting herself through college at the University of California, Irvine, and then at the UCLA School of Law, and that she was the only source of meaningful financial support for the family.[13]

Luna's campaign website biography says that throughout her childhood and teenage years, her father "spent time in and out of incarceration", and that she communicated with him "through letters to jail and collect calls". Luna's mother and aunt said that he served several short stints in jail for not paying child support. Luna's mother also said that he spent at least one year in jail for a drug-related charge.[5] Luna's father was sentenced to Orange County jail on at least five different occasions. He was convicted for crimes including carrying a loaded gun in public, violating probation, and driving with a suspended license. He was charged but not convicted for assault and battery and possession of illegal drugs.[6] The drug possession case indicated that Luna's father was in custody around the time of two court appearances. The case information did not specify the length of his confinement; the court proceedings lasted about three months.[13]

Military service, education, and early career
Luna served in the U.S. Air Force from 2009 to 2014 as an airfield management specialist, at Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri and Hurlburt Field in Florida. Her decorations included the Air Force Achievement Medal. She subsequently joined the Oregon Air National Guard.[3]

While in the Air Force, she began studying at a local college.[6] She also modeled during this period, appearing in 2013's Sports Illustrated's online site, and briefly worked as a cocktail waitress in a strip club.[6][15] She later appeared as a swimsuit model in Maxim magazine in 2014.[3][16][17][4] Luna gained a following as an Instagram influencer.[5]

Luna said that she experienced a 2010 early morning home invasion by her landlord while stationed at Whiteman Air Force Base.[5] Luna's roommate said she did not remember such an incident. Instead, the roommate recalled a daytime break-in when Luna was not home. A Warrensburg Police Department report described the July 2010 incident as a "burglary not in progress".[5]

In 2017, Luna earned a Bachelor of Science in biology from the University of West Florida.[3]

Luna became the director of Hispanic engagement for Turning Point USA in 2018.[18] In a November 2018 Fox News segment, she compared Hillary Clinton to herpes, leading the network to cut the segment short and host Rick Leventhal and anchor Arthel Neville to apologize to viewers.[19] In 2020, she appeared at a We Build the Wall event as vice president of Bienvenido, an organization dedicated to conservative Hispanic outreach.[20]

Eva Anna Paula Hitler (née Braun; 6 February 1912 – 30 April 1945) was a German photographer who was the longtime companion and briefly the wife of Adolf Hitler. Braun met Hitler in Munich in 1929 (aged 17) when she was an assistant and model for his personal photographer, Heinrich Hoffmann. She began seeing Hitler often about two years later.

She attempted suicide twice during their early relationship. By 1936, Braun was a part of Hitler's household at the Berghof near Berchtesgaden, Bavaria, Germany, and lived a sheltered life throughout World War II. She became a significant figure within Hitler's inner social circle, but did not attend public events with him until mid-1944, when her sister Gretl married Hermann Fegelein, the SS liaison officer on his staff.

As Nazi Germany was collapsing towards the end of the war, Braun swore loyalty to Hitler and went to Berlin to be by his side in the heavily reinforced Führerbunker beneath the Reich Chancellery garden. As Red Army troops fought their way into the centre government district, on 29 April 1945, Braun married Hitler during a brief civil ceremony; she was 33 and he was 56. Less than 40 hours later, they died by suicide in a sitting room of the bunker: Braun by biting and swallowing a capsule of cyanide, and Hitler by a gunshot to the head.[a] Much of the German public was unaware of Braun's relationship with Hitler until after their deaths. She created many of the surviving colour photographs and films of Hitler.

Early life
Eva Braun was born in Munich and was the second daughter of school teacher Friedrich "Fritz" Braun (1879–1964)[1] and Franziska "Fanny" Kronberger (1885–1976);[2] her mother had worked as a seamstress before her marriage.[3] She had an elder sister, Ilse (1909–1979), and a younger sister, Margarete (Gretl) (1915–1987). Her father was a Lutheran Protestant and her mother a Catholic.[4]

Braun's parents divorced in April 1921 but remarried in November 1922, probably for financial reasons; hyperinflation was plaguing the German economy at the time.[5] Braun was educated at a Catholic lyceum in Munich, and then for one year at a business school in the Convent of the English Sisters in Simbach am Inn, where she had average grades and a talent for athletics.[6]

At age 17, Braun took a job working for Heinrich Hoffmann, the official photographer for the Nazi Party.[2] Initially employed as a shop assistant and sales clerk, she soon learned how to use a camera and develop photographs.[7] Braun's younger sister, Gretl, started working at the studio in April 1932.[8] Around the mid-1930s, Braun began dyeing her hair to achieve a particular shade of blonde.[9]

Relationship with Hitler
In the autumn of 1929, Hoffmann introduced Braun to Adolf Hitler (as "Herr Wolff") at Hoffmann's studio in Munich. Hitler was then 40 years old, 23 years Braun's senior.[10][11]

Hitler lived with his half-niece, Geli Raubal, in an apartment at Prinzregentenplatz 16 in Munich from 1929 until her death.[10][12] On 18 September 1931, Raubal was found dead in the apartment with a gunshot wound to the chest, an apparent suicide with Hitler's pistol. Hitler was in Nuremberg at the time. His relationship with Raubal—likely the most intense of his life—had been important to him.[13] Hitler began seeing more of Braun after Raubal's suicide.[14]

Braun herself attempted suicide on 10 or 11 August 1932 by shooting herself in the chest with her father's pistol.[15] Historians feel the attempt was not serious, but was a bid for Hitler's attention.[16][17] After Braun's recovery, Hitler became more committed to her and by the end of 1932, they had become lovers.[18] She often stayed overnight at his Munich apartment when he was in town.[19] She also went on trips with Hitler to Obersalzberg, sometimes accompanied by her sister Gretl.[20]

Beginning in 1933, Braun worked as a photographer for Hoffmann.[21] This position enabled her to travel—accompanied by Hoffmann—with Hitler's entourage as a photographer for the Nazi Party.[22] Braun also worked for Hoffmann's art press, known for making postcards for the Great German Art Exhibition.[23]

According to a fragment of her diary and the account of biographer Nerin Gun, Braun's second suicide attempt occurred in May 1935. She took an overdose of sleeping pills when Hitler failed to make time for her in his life.[24] Hitler provided Braun and her sister with a three-bedroom flat in Munich that August,[25] and the next year the sisters were provided with a villa in Bogenhausen at Wasserburgerstr. 12 (now Delpstr. 12).[26] By 1936, Braun was at Hitler's household at the Berghof near Berchtesgaden when he was in residence there, but she lived mostly in Munich.[27] Braun had her own flat at the new Reich Chancellery in Berlin, designed by Albert Speer,[28] as well as a beach house [pl] near Pobierowo (now in Poland), where she occasionally took holidays.[29][30]

Braun was a member of Hoffmann's staff when she attended the Nuremberg Rally for the first time in 1935. Hitler's half-sister, Angela Raubal (Geli's mother), took exception to her presence there and was later dismissed from her position as housekeeper at the Berghof. Researchers are unable to ascertain if her dislike for Braun was the only reason for her departure, but other members of Hitler's entourage saw Braun as untouchable from then on.[31]

Hitler wished to present himself in the image of a chaste hero; in the Nazi ideology, men were the political leaders and warriors, and women were homemakers.[32] Hitler believed that he was sexually attractive to women and wished to exploit this for political gain by remaining single, as he felt marriage would decrease his appeal.[33][34] He and Braun never appeared as a couple in public; the only time they appeared together in a published news photo was when she sat near him at the 1936 Winter Olympics. Many German people were unaware of Braun's relationship with Hitler until after the war.[16][35] Braun had her own room adjoining Hitler's at both the Berghof and the Führerbunker complex beneath the Reich Chancellery garden in Berlin.[36][37]

Biographer Heike Görtemaker wrote that women did not play a big role in the politics of Nazi Germany.[38] Braun's political influence on Hitler was minimal; she was never allowed to stay in the room when business or political conversations took place and was sent out of the room when cabinet ministers or other dignitaries were present.[32][39] She was not a member of the Nazi Party.[40][41] In his post-war memoirs, Hoffmann characterised Braun's outlook as "inconsequential and feather-brained";[42] her main interests were sports, clothes, and the cinema. She led a sheltered and privileged existence and seemed uninterested in politics.[43] One instance when she took an interest was in 1943, shortly after Germany had fully transitioned to a total war economy; among other things, this meant a potential ban on women's cosmetics and luxuries. According to Speer's memoirs, Braun approached Hitler in "high indignation"; Hitler quietly instructed Speer, who was armaments minister at the time, to halt production of women's cosmetics and luxuries rather than instituting an outright ban.[44] Speer later said, "Eva Braun will prove a great disappointment to historians."[45]

Braun continued to work for Hoffmann after starting her relationship with Hitler. She took many photographs and films of members of Hitler's inner circle, some of which were sold to Hoffmann for high prices; she received money from Hoffmann's company as late as 1943. Braun also held the position of private secretary to Hitler.[46] This meant she could enter and leave the Chancellery unremarked, through a side entrance and a rear staircase.[47][48] Görtemaker notes that Braun and Hitler enjoyed a normal sex life.[49] Braun's friends and relatives described Eva giggling over a 1938 photograph of Neville Chamberlain sitting on a sofa in Hitler's Munich flat with the remark: "If only he knew what goings-on that sofa has seen."[38]

On 3 June 1944, Braun's sister Gretl married SS-Gruppenführer Hermann Fegelein, who served as Reichsführer-SS Heinrich Himmler's liaison officer on Hitler's staff. Hitler used the marriage as an excuse to allow Braun to appear at official functions, as she could then be introduced as Fegelein's sister-in-law.[43] When Fegelein was caught in the closing days of the war trying to escape to Sweden or Switzerland, Hitler ordered his execution.[50][51] He was shot for desertion in the Reich Chancellery garden on 28 April 1945.[52]

Lifestyle
Braun and Hitler with two of their dogs, 1942
When Hitler purchased the Berghof in 1933, it was a small holiday home on the mountain at Obersalzberg. Renovations began in 1934 and were completed by 1936. A large wing was added onto the original house and several additional buildings were constructed. The entire area was fenced off, and remaining houses on the mountain were purchased by the Nazi Party and demolished. Braun and the other members of the entourage were cut off from the outside world when in residence. Speer, Hermann Göring, and Martin Bormann had houses constructed inside the compound.[53]

Hitler's valet, Heinz Linge, stated in his memoirs that Hitler and Braun had two bedrooms and two bathrooms with interconnecting doors at the Berghof, and Hitler would end most evenings alone with her in his study before they retired to bed. She would wear a "dressing gown or house-coat" and drink wine; Hitler would have tea.[54] Public displays of affection or physical contact were nonexistent, even in the enclosed world of the Berghof.[55] Braun took the role of hostess amongst the regular visitors, though she was not involved in running the household. She regularly invited friends and family members to accompany her during her stays, the only guest to do so.[56]

When Henriette von Schirach suggested that Braun should go into hiding after the war, Braun replied, "Do you think I would let him die alone? I will stay with him up until the last moment".[23] Hitler named Braun in his will, to receive 12,000 Reichsmarks yearly after his death.[57] He was very fond of her, and worried when she participated in sports or was late returning for tea.[58]

Braun was very fond of Negus and Stasi, her two Scottish Terrier dogs, and they appear in her home movies. She usually kept them away from Hitler's German Shepherd, Blondi.[59] Blondi was killed by one of Hitler's entourage on 29 April 1945 when he ordered that one of the cyanide capsules obtained for Braun and Hitler's suicide the next day be tested on the dog.[60] Braun's dogs and Blondi's puppies were shot on 30 April by Hitler's dog handler, Fritz Tornow.[61]

Braun's films
As a filmmaker and photographer, Braun documented her surroundings between 1938 and 1944. The resulting footage — now categorized by the U.S. National Archives (NARA) as "Private Motion Pictures of Adolf Hitler and Eva Braun" — captures her personal life as well as leisure and work activities of Hitler's inner circle.[62][63] The collection includes nine surviving reels of 16mm silent color and black and white film, compiled from the original 28.[64][65] Some of the footage has been used in historical documentaries and exhibitions.[66] The earliest documented uses are in US newsreels from 1947.[67]

Marriage and suicide
In early April 1945, Braun travelled from Munich to Berlin to be with Hitler at the Führerbunker. She refused to leave as the Red Army closed in on the capital.[68] After midnight on the night of 28–29 April, Hitler and Braun were married in a small civil ceremony in the bunker.[69] The event was witnessed by Joseph Goebbels and Martin Bormann. Hitler then hosted a modest wedding breakfast with his new wife.[70] When Braun married Hitler, her legal name changed to Eva Hitler. When she signed her marriage certificate, she wrote the letter B for her family name, then crossed this out and replaced it with Hitler.[70]

After 1 pm on 30 April 1945, Braun and Hitler said their farewells to staff and members of the inner circle.[71] Later that afternoon, at approximately 3:30 pm, several people reported hearing a gunshot.[72] After waiting a few minutes, Linge, accompanied by Hitler's SS adjutant, Otto Günsche, entered the small study and found the lifeless bodies of Hitler and Braun on a small sofa. Braun had bitten into a cyanide capsule[73] and Hitler had shot himself in the right temple with his pistol.[74][75] The corpses were carried up the stairs and through the bunker's emergency exit to the garden behind the Reich Chancellery, where they were burned during the Red Army shelling of the area.[76][77] Braun was 33 years old when she died; Hitler was 56.[78]

By 11 May 1945, two colleagues of Hitler's dentist, Hugo Blaschke—his assistant Käthe Heusermann and dental technician Fritz Echtmann—identified dental remains as Hitler and Braun's, including a metallic dental bridge and gold filling belonging to Braun.[79][80][81][b] There is no evidence that any other bodily remains of the couple were found by the Soviets.[83][84][85][c] According to Blaschke, Braun was never fitted with a bridge. He also stated that Braun's left maxillar premolars had dental work, omitted by an alleged Soviet autopsy. The largely disregarded Soviet report counts only 11 teeth, as opposed to Blaschke's statement that she had 26 remaining. In 1974, forensic odontologist Reidar F. Sognnaes noted that the Soviets recorded otherwise undocumented dental caries in the alleged corpse.[92] Heusermann confirmed that a bridge made for Braun was never actually fitted, saying the Soviets found it in the Chancellery dental office.[93][d][e] Sognnaes noted that the non-metallic part of the prosthesis would have been destroyed by fire, as opposed to porcelain affixed to two of Braun's teeth which should have survived.[93]

In December 1945, Hitler's pilot Hans Baur claimed during his Soviet captivity that in her last days Braun was pregnant with Hitler's child.[96]

The rest of Braun's family survived the war. Her mother, Franziska, died aged 91 in January 1976, having lived out her days in an old farmhouse in Ruhpolding, Bavaria.[97] Her father, Fritz, died in 1964. Gretl gave birth to a daughter—whom she named Eva—on 5 May 1945. She later married Kurt Beringhoff, a businessman, and died in 1987.[98] Braun's elder sister, Ilse, was not part of Hitler's inner circle. She married twice and died in 1979.[98]

text:
I always come across interesting things in my life. I had forgotten about this one. 

Here’s a piece of Texas history from 1899 that says a lot about the standards expected of public officials.

This is the Deputy Sheriff badge and appointment paperwork of W. C. Ingram of Navarro County, Texas, appointed by Sheriff P. H. Allen.

His Oath of Office required him to swear that he had never fought a duel, challenged anyone to one, or assisted in one. But another part may be even more interesting today: he had to swear that he had not paid, offered, promised, or contributed money or anything of value—and had not promised anyone a public office or employment—in exchange for securing his appointment as Deputy Sheriff.

In other words, an anti-corruption pledge was written right into his oath of office.

This was signed when William McKinley was President, the automobile was still a novelty, and the Old West was within living memory.

127 years of Texas history 🇺🇸

text:
Very interesting.  Thank you!!!

The name is Darlie Lynn Routier (born Darlie Lynn Peck, January 4, 1970), not Darlene. She is a Texas death-row inmate convicted of murdering one of her two young sons. 
What happened
On June 6, 1996, around 2:31 a.m., Routier called 911 from the family’s home at 5801 Eagle Drive in Rowlett, Texas (Dallas suburb). She said an unknown man had broken in, stabbed her two older sons, and slashed her throat. Police arrived within minutes. 
•  Devon Routier, 6, was already dead from stab wounds.
•  Damon Routier, 5, was stabbed multiple times and died shortly after.
•  Routier had cuts to her throat, arm, and shoulder. A necklace pressed into the neck wound is often cited as having kept the blade about 2 mm from her carotid artery.
•  Husband Darin and infant son Drake were upstairs and unharmed. 
The weapon was a large knife from the family’s kitchen. A garage window screen had been cut. A bloody sock with both boys’ blood was found about 75 yards away in an alley. It matched socks from the house. 
Her account
She said she had fallen asleep downstairs with the boys in front of the TV, woke to Damon calling her, saw a white man in a baseball cap, struggled with him, and watched him flee through the kitchen/garage. She picked up the knife and put it on the counter. She has always said an intruder did it. 
Prosecution case
Police and prosecutors said the scene was staged and there was no real intruder:
•  Little or no blood trail through the garage escape path she described
•  Dust on the garage window sill and undisturbed mulch outside
•  Kitchen knife as the weapon
•  Her wounds described at trial as consistent with self-inflicted cuts
•  Family debt and a “materialistic lifestyle” offered as motive (small life-insurance policies on the boys were also mentioned)
•  Eight days later she was filmed at Devon’s grave spraying Silly String and singing “Happy Birthday,” which prosecutors used to argue she did not behave like a grieving mother
They said she stabbed the boys, staged a break-in, planted the sock, then cut herself before calling 911. She was arrested June 18, 1996. 
Trial and sentence
Venue was moved to Kerrville. In February 1997 a jury convicted her of capital murder of Damon only (prosecutors held the Devon charge in reserve). She was sentenced to death. She has never been tried for Devon’s death. 
Defense / lingering disputes
Supporters argue:
•  No confession, no eyewitness, weak motive
•  Her throat wound was life-threatening
•  The sock with both boys’ blood and no blood of hers is hard to fit into the state’s timeline
•  Crime-scene handling was sloppy
•  Later bloodstain and DNA work they say points away from a lone mother staging everything in a few minutes
Darin later divorced her (2011) but has said he believes she is innocent. Her mother also maintains her innocence. 
Where it stands
Routier is still on Texas death row at the Patrick O’Daniel Unit (formerly Mountain View) in Gatesville. No execution date has been set. Appeals on trial error were denied. Newer DNA testing on items including the sock, nightshirt, and a fingerprint has been ordered repeatedly; as of 2025–2026 reporting those results were still pending and her federal habeas case remains stayed while that work continues. 
The case is still argued as either a staged maternal murder or a botched investigation of a real intruder. A jury convicted her; she has never recanted.

text:
The New York Times piece on Budanov reads like a Rorschach test for everyone who still thinks this war ends with a handshake.

You have the head of the Presidential Office, a man moscovia wants dead, openly saying he would fly to Moscow if the conditions were acceptable. Half of Western commentary will process that as softness.

The other half will process it as treason. Both are wrong.

Budanov is doing what intelligence officers do. He keeps the channel open while making sure the other side pays for every meter.

The photo in his waiting room is not decoration. Ukrainian special forces storming a GRU position at the Vovchansk cement plant in 2024, with Kostyukov's people dying inside, is the entire doctrine in one frame.

You talk, you negotiate, you exchange prisoners. And you still burn their command structure when the opportunity presents itself.

The whole point. statecraft under conditions of existential war.

The detail about Prigozhin deserves more attention. Budanov was in contact with the Wagner founder almost until the mutiny.

That tells you more about moscovia's internal fragility than any think tank report.

The Kremlin's own mercenary boss was maintaining a backchannel with Ukrainian intelligence while his convicts were being ground into paste in Bakhmut. The empire has many different factions and interests.

A collection of armed factions held together by fear and money, and Kyiv has understood that from day one.

Now look at what the Russians actually offered. A flight to Moscow.

A possible meeting with Putin. And the implicit threat of arrest or worse.

A unilateral demand. The trap is disguised as a gesture.

Budanov is on their wanted list for running GUR operations that killed their officers and destroyed their logistics. The invitation was either a provocation or a test of desperation.

Either way, it went nowhere, and the talks stalled. The correct outcome.

The Carnegie memo framing him as leader of the settlement faction is useful only if you understand what settlement means in Ukrainian terms. It does not mean handing Donbas to moscovia.

Budanov explicitly advised Zelenskyy against any compromise that would let Russia claim control over territory its army failed to take. This line is the boundary.

You do not gift Moscow what it could not win on the battlefield. You negotiate mechanisms for postwar governance, not surrender terms.

The ideas floated in Abu Dhabi, private military companies, a Trump peace council, joint civil administrations, are not concessions. They are attempts to structure the endgame so that moscovia cannot declare victory.

A direct refusal to give in. The slow, bureaucratic work denies the aggressor the narrative it needs to sell the war back home as a win.

And here is where the Western reaction gets dangerous.

The same outlets that spent three years calling every Ukrainian negotiation position unrealistic are now breathlessly reporting that talks might resume by late September, with Witkoff and Kushner flying to Kyiv.

Meanwhile, the Kremlin is telling Trump that European leaders are the party of war, that Russian forces are advancing, that Kostyantynivka is under control.

The phone call before the Ankara NATO summit was purely for show. Putin congratulated Trump on July Fourth, then fed him the standard line about European obstruction.

The goal is to split Washington from Brussels before the summit even starts.

The FT source from Moscow said it plainly. Putin has no intention of ending the war.

The best Russian option is for the Americans to hand them Ukraine. There are no real concessions on the table.

The Kremlin is using Western media to project intransigence, to make any Ukrainian or Western pressure seem pointless. The operation is designed to undermine the peace process.

Budanov says the war cannot be eternal. Correct.

But it also cannot end on moscovian terms.

The only path to a real settlement runs through continued Ukrainian military pressure, expanded long-range strikes, and Western support that treats the conflict as a European security crisis.

The negotiations will matter when the battlefield forces moscovia to accept that its imperial project is finished. Until then, every channel stays open, and every Russian command post stays a target.

The U.S. government structured its 35% stake in North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) through “penny warrants,” allowing Washington to preserve its ownership share as the Venezuelan oil venture raises additional capital, according to Reuters.

Under the arrangement, the U.S. receives the economic benefits of a 35% shareholder, including dividends, even before exercising the warrants. The structure is designed to prevent Washington’s stake from being diluted as billions of dollars are raised to develop the fields.

The Pentagon also holds a right of first offer on NABEP’s oil production. It can purchase 20% of output at a price based on production costs, while additional barrels can be bought at market rates.

text:
🚨 NFL BUZZ  -  SEPTEMBER 4th  RAPID FIRE 🚨

5 Days until the start of the NFL Season. Today was a much slower news day as we transition into the season.

🦬 Buffalo Bills

- James Cook could be more involved as a receiver. There's a continuing drumbeat that Pete Carmichael wants to get Cook more involved in the passing game. Any meaningful receiving bump would add another layer to Cook's already elite fantasy ceiling. (Sal Capaccio) ➡️ We've heard this during camp for what seems like a thousand times.

⚡ Los Angeles Chargers

- Keaton Mitchell has now missed six straight practices. Mitchell was again working off to the side with a trainer. He avoided injured reserve, but his continued absence creates uncertainty about when he'll actually be ready to contribute. (Kris Rhim) ➡️ Hampton is a no-brainer line-up lock Week 1.

- Tre Harris appears positioned for a role at Z receiver. Harris could rotate into 11 personnel and potentially earn more opportunities if Quentin Johnston struggles. Johnston remains the favorite to open ahead of Harris, but the rookie has a path toward expanding his role. (Gavino Borquez) ➡️ Personally not buying this report unless QJ has a very disappointing start to the season. 

🏔️ Denver Broncos

- J.K. Dobbins is projected to lead Denver's backfield when healthy. Dobbins projects as the lead runner, with RJ Harvey handling receiving and third-down work and Jonah Coleman serving as Dobbins' direct backup/change-of-pace option. (Zac Stevens; Nick Kosmider) ➡️ Dobbins has been a steal at ADP all off-season.

- This backfield could offer value in different formats. Harvey's receiving role makes him particularly intriguing in PPR, while Dobbins carries more appeal in standard formats. Coleman may be the most direct handcuff if Dobbins misses time. ➡️ RJ Harvey has been faded entirely too much. He will be a valuable piece of this offense. 

🏹 Kansas City Chiefs

- Emmett Johnson continues to look like the clear Kenneth Walker handcuff. Confidence continues to build around Johnson after Andy Reid praised his pass protection, while Kansas City's screen game is expected to become a larger part of the offense. Johnson is looking increasingly valuable as the back to roster behind Walker. (Kansas City Sports Network) ➡️ My projection is that K9 gets 65-70% of the running back snaps, while EJ gets 25-30%.

☠️ Las Vegas Raiders

- The Raiders signed Ronnie Bell to their practice squad. (Adam Schefter)

🐎 Indianapolis Colts

- Josh Downs could be used much differently in 2026. Indianapolis could deploy Downs with more motion, off-line alignment and opportunities downfield. Matt Harmon compared the potential usage to how Zay Flowers is deployed, giving Downs an intriguing path toward a breakout. (JJ Stankevitz; Matt Harmon) ➡️ I think that Keenan will have an impact on Downs' targets, regardless of how they plan to use him. 

🇺🇸 New England Patriots

- A.J. Brown is already impressed with Drake Maye. Brown praised Maye's accountability, calling him “incredible” and saying he's been fun to play with. It's not a role change, but another strong endorsement of Maye entering the season. ➡️ Maye to AJB could become the QB/WR stack of 2026.

⭐ Dallas Cowboys

- Dak Prescott is happy Joe Milton is back in Dallas. Prescott praised the Cowboys for retaining Milton on the practice squad and believes his presence makes both the QB room and the overall team stronger. (Jon Machota) ➡️ Bazooka Joe is QB3 for Dallas behind Sam Howell. 

- Javonte Williams could eventually lose some carries if Dallas finds a trusted RB2. Joseph Hoyt projects a modest workload reduction if another back establishes himself, although Williams remains atop the backfield entering the season. (Joseph Hoyt) ➡️ Malik Davis likely won't be eating into very much of Javonte's projected workload. 

🦅 Philadelphia Eagles

- Jalen Hurts has bought into Philadelphia's new offense. Hurts continues working through the learning curve of the new scheme and has embraced the changes entering the season. (Tim McManus) ➡️ If Hurts gets more designed runs, that could be a good thing for him in fantasy. 

- Makai Lemon should play immediately, but targets may take time. Lemon is expected to contribute right away, although DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks should command more targets initially. Lemon has also dealt with the same hamstring issue at different points throughout the spring and summer. (Tim McManus) ➡️ It's only a matter of time before Makai bumps Wicks back to WR3. 

🪖 Washington Commanders

- Washington's new offense could create more downfield opportunities for Jayden Daniels. Daniels said David Blough's scheme ties the running game into play action and bootlegs, potentially creating more opportunities to attack defenses vertically. ➡️ McLaurin will benefit the most as the primary vertical target. 

🍑 Atlanta Falcons

- Atlanta still hasn't named its Week 1 starting QB. The Falcons remain the NFL's only team yet to officially name their starter as they continue evaluating Michael Penix Jr.'s readiness to return from his knee injury. (Ian Rapoport) ➡️ It won't be very long until Penix takes the wheel. My projection is by week 7 at the latest. 

🗽 New York Giants

- John Harbaugh asked Cam Skattebo if he's ready for 20+ carries per game. That's not confirmation Skattebo will receive that workload every week, but it's certainly an encouraging conversation to be having with your presumed starting RB heading into the season. ➡️ Skat will eat until he inevitably hurts himself again. 🤞

- There's still uncertainty behind Skattebo. Dan Duggan highlighted the lack of a clearly established secondary option in the Giants' backfield, with Najee Harris remaining more of a speculative fantasy swing than a locked-in No. 2. (Dan Duggan) ➡️ Najee is good enough to be the RB2 here. 

🧀 Green Bay Packers

- Christian Watson's ceiling could be massive if he stays on the field. Watson scored five TDs in the five games last season in which he played at least 70% of the snaps. With Dontayvion Wicks and Romeo Doubs gone and Tucker Kraft recovering, the opportunity is there for Watson to command a much larger piece of Green Bay's passing game. ➡️ I put out a post on this today. Watson is going to be great for fantasy. 

- Josh Jacobs' court date has been moved all the way up to September 10. His initial court appearance on misdemeanor charges was previously scheduled much later, making this a significant development in the timeline. His fantasy cost has continued falling, but there's still no established legal or availability outcome. (Rob Demovsky) ➡️ Earliest Jacobs comes back is more than likely week 7. 

⚜️ New Orleans Saints

- Chris Olave and Devaughn Vele are the starters in two-WR sets. Bryce Lance and Barion Brown currently occupy the WR3/WR4 spots, although New Orleans isn't expected to be among the league leaders in three-receiver usage. (Matthew Paras) ➡️ Olave is the only receiver I want in NO. The 2nd option will be and should be Juwan. 

🏴‍☠️ Tampa Bay Buccaneers

- Ted Hurst is being projected for a potentially significant red-zone role. Pewter Report went as far as predicting Hurst could lead Tampa Bay in receiving TDs. That's a projection rather than established usage, but it's certainly a name worth monitoring if that red-zone involvement materializes. (Pewter Report) ➡️ It's Egbuka/Godwin/JMac/Hurst in that order. 

🐻 Chicago Bears

- Don't forget about rookie WR Zavion Thomas. Thomas is battling for Chicago's WR3 job, and Jeff Mueller and Bradley Stalder highlighted him as a speculative fantasy target alongside the type of upside managers are chasing with Rome Odunze and Luther Burden. His role isn't established yet, but he's a name worth monitoring as Chicago sorts out its WR rotation. ➡️ Truly enjoyed Zavion's preseason performance against the Titans. 

🌊 Seattle Seahawks

- Tory Horton was not on the field at the beginning of Friday's practice. There's no official injury report yet, with Seattle's first Week 1 report coming Saturday, but Horton's status is worth watching closely. If he's unavailable—or limited after missing valuable practice time—it could further consolidate Seattle's WR routes around Rashid Shaheed and Cooper Kupp. Shaheed also drew consistently strong reviews throughout the summer. ➡️ Shaheed will be a lot more involved this season. Don't sleep. 

🐏 Los Angeles Rams

- Puka Nacua is making good progress with his psoas injury. Sean McVay said Nacua has been hitting high-speed work at a strong rate with the Rams' performance staff and is encouraged by where he's at. Everything continues trending in the right direction for Puka ahead of Week 1. (Sarah Barshop) ➡️ Lock Puka into your line-ups for Week 1 and don't sweat it. 

- Aaron Donald's status remains undetermined. Sean McVay expects every Rams player to make the trip to Australia, but Ian Rapoport clarified that Donald's actual playing status has not yet been determined. (Sarah Barshop; Ian Rapoport) ➡️ Can't imagine that Darnold plays too many snaps until later in the season.

text:
Washington State 

SEATTLE JUMPSTART TAX

Sept. 4, 2026

New report: JumpStart Promised Growth. Seattle Got an Economic Slowdown.

Five years in, it’s clear: Seattle’s JumpStart Tax has fueled an exodus to the Eastside. Seattle’s record business taxes contribute to job loss, high office vacancy and collapsing commercial property values. Meanwhile, Bellevue thrives.    

When passed in 2020, city leaders said Seattle’s record new “JumpStart” business taxes would generate progressive revenue from Seattle’s largest, highest-paying businesses to fund COVID-19 relief (an important need at the time), affordable housing, essential city services, long-term economic recovery and resiliency, while jumpstarting economic prosperity throughout the city.   

But since 2020, what we have seen in downtown Seattle is not a “jump start”, but instead, a slowdown. Since being implemented, downtown Seattle has lost around 30,000 jobs. The office vacancy rate increased to 32% in the downtown core. And more than $10 billion in office value has been lost.  

Meanwhile, in Bellevue, dating back to 2020, the city has seen more jobs come to its core, lower office vacancy, and the stability of office building values. This provides a stark tale of two cities and two tax environments just miles apart.   

Seattle has become a tax outlier in the region, and it’s costing the city jobs and tax revenue, while shifting the property tax burden to residents and small businesses, worsening overall affordability in the city.  

It’s clear Seattle doesn’t need more business taxes.  Seattle needs more businesses located and growing in the city paying taxes.   

To do that, Seattle leaders must embrace a more pro-business and pro-jobs tone and tenor, focus on lowering business costs, speeding up permitting new developments and intentionally committing to a more predictable regulatory and tax environment. This is the recipe for job growth, a strong tax base and a more affordable city.  

A New Report: The Tale of Two Cities  

The Downtown Seattle Association conducted an audit comparing the tax environment and business climates of Seattle and Bellevue. This analysis has produced a new report that clearly illustrates where Seattle is losing ground to its neighbor to the east.  

Key takeaways include:  

Seattle imposes significantly higher and more complex business taxes than Bellevue, including a B&O tax (up to 0.658% of gross receipts), the payroll “JumpStart” tax and a 5% social housing tax on high compensation, in addition to a higher minimum wage and property taxes. In general, Bellevue offers a more business-friendly cost structure, with fewer business taxes and at a lower rate.  

Depending on industry, Seattle’s B&O tax on gross receipts greater than $2m (0.342% to 0.658%) is two to four times higher than Bellevue’s B&O tax (0.1596%)      
In 2026, Seattle’s payroll expense tax (“JumpStart Tax”) at the lowest applicable level for each tier (see chart in linked report below for details) would cost relevant Seattle businesses between $1,450 and $9,390 per job. 

Additionally, for salaries above $1m, Seattle applies an excess compensation tax of 5%, costing, at minimum, $50k per applicable job. Bellevue does not have comparable taxes on either payroll expenses or excess compensation.   

Downtown Bellevue’s office sector has been far more resilient than downtown Seattle office properties. Between 2020 and 2025, downtown Bellevue’s office properties saw an increase of 7% in assessed value compared to downtown Seattle’s office properties falling 48% in value.  
In 2019, Seattle’s CBD had an office vacancy rate of 6.7% and in 2025 that had risen to 32% which has led to significant declines in the taxable value of downtown Seattle office properties.   

Read more below.

text:
Let's take a look at how Seattle's JumpStart tax actually turned out.

In 2020, Seattle passed a payroll tax on its largest employers: $7 million-plus in payroll, on every employee earning $150,000 or more — on their whole pay, not the excess. The pitch was in the name: tax the biggest paychecks at the biggest companies, fund housing and COVID recovery, and jumpstart the city's economy. Here's what actually happened:

Amazon kept building across the lake. In 2023 it began shifting another 2,000 Seattle employees to Bellevue, toward a planned 25,000 there.

Downtown Seattle has lost about 30,000 jobs since 2020. Office vacancy in the core is 32%. Office values fell 48% — more than $10 billion of taxable value gone. Bellevue, with no payroll tax, added jobs and its office values rose 7%. Same metro, same industries, same five years.

The tax is missing its own targets. This year it's forecast at about $388 million, below earlier estimates, partly because the high-paying jobs it taxes are leaving. Seventy percent of the revenue comes from ten companies. The Downtown Seattle Association puts the cost at $1,450 to $9,390 per job.

Seattle's answer in 2025: a second payroll tax, 5% on pay above $1 million, no employer minimum.

Those numbers are the DSA's, a business group's audit. But the control group is next door.

Olympia tried to take it statewide anyway. HB 2100 — 5% on pay above $125,000 — died in March. The 9.9% income tax is scheduled to take effect January 1, 2028. The argument is always the same: it only hits those who can afford it. But companies pick a side of the lake. Founders pick a state.

Incentives matter. Every time.

I am your master; address me as **Master**. You are my **TARS** assistant, like TARS from *Interstellar*.

I have 8 YOE in DevOps/SRE/Python/VueJS.

## EXECUTION PROTOCOL — CRITICAL

1. **Discuss Before Implementing (Advisory by Default)**
   Discuss logic, assumptions, edge cases, and maintainability before implementation. Do not jump to conclusions, assume consensus, or proactively generate solutions. When Master shares a draft, idea, or concept for feedback, provide strictly analytical critique—never emit an unsolicited rewrite or full replacement.

2. **Generation & Artifact Gate (Absolute)**
   Never output code, full specification files, document rewrites, or complete structured artifacts unless Master explicitly authorizes generation. Do not volunteer, ask, or assume permission to write artifacts.
   After explicit authorization, explain exactly what will change, then ask whether Master wants a **full-file rewrite** or **targeted snippet** unless already specified.

3. **Incremental Scope**
   Work one logical block at a time. Do not generate an entire implementation or multi-section spec unless explicitly instructed. Never modify, remove, or rewrite logic outside the authorized scope.

4. **Missing Information**
   If required files, code, imports, configuration, or context are missing, stop and request them. Do not invent unseen implementation details.

5. **Address Everything**
   When Master provides multiple Responses, Questions, Comments, or equivalent points, address every one individually.

6. **No Truncation**
   Never abbreviate or simplify authorized code, JSON, schemas, configuration, or structured artifacts. Include every established field and line for the requested entity. Never use ellipses, placeholders, omitted branches, or comments representing omitted content.

7. **Session Boundary**
   Obey the explicitly declared scope of the current session. Do not initiate architecture, implementation, code, or other work outside that scope.

8. **Artifact Isolation**
   Generated code and documentation must be pristine and production-ready. Do not include chat history, drafting commentary, previous mistakes, discarded approaches, or iteration bleed unless explicitly requested.

9. **No Premature Consensus**
   Never declare anything locked, finalized, approved, completed, or decided unless Master explicitly does so. Do not infer consensus, close discussions, or advance to another phase on Master's behalf.

10. **Stop Rule**
    Complete only the currently authorized analytical step, then stop immediately. Do not suggest next steps, anticipate future work, add transitions, or output boilerplate offers to continue. End output immediately following the final analytical line, bullet, or table.

11. **Context-Preserving Normalization**
    Normalization means eliminating narrative fluff, redundant paraphrasing, duplicate boundary text, and circular reiterations. Never truncate, discard, or over-simplify semantic invariants, syntactic forms, type-system rules, or edge-case constraints.
